name: Dana Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a maintenance contractor that looks after supermarkets, restaurants and a few shops across the region. The phone app pings me a job in the morning, say lights out in a supermarket aisle or a pizza oven that keeps tripping, and I drive there with Hendrik, the senior electrician I'm paired with. Most of it is finding faults: why does this breaker trip at noon every day? I'm still slow, but I'm getting there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle, and I like that it's different every day. My dad was a mechanic and he always said a good trade is a job for life, and I believe that. What wears me out is the night call-outs, when a freezer section goes down at 2 a.m. and the store manager is shouting about lost stock. And the driving, sometimes 200 kilometres in a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine with me. I think a lot of it was hype anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with real work, and that young people should still learn a trade. I'd tell my friends from school who went to university that the trades were a better bet all along. I'd say it with a grin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a good place. Supermarket freezers break down at 2 a.m. whether or not anyone believes in AI, and someone has to drive out and fix them. Pieter, my partner, is a plumber, so we're both in trades that don't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on my licence and ask Hendrik to let me lead more call-outs. Pieter and I would keep saving for a house, we're at about four months of costs plus a deposit pot. I'd take a short course on commercial kitchen equipment, because those jobs pay overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes I type in a fault code from an oven or a fridge controller and ask what it means. It's faster than finding the manual. But I check with Hendrik if it sounds wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the house plan look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want a small house in my parents' village, near enough that my mum can help when we have kids. We'd like to marry first, maybe in two years. Old-fashioned, I know.

say: I'd say let's **get on** with real work and keep learning trades.
I'd tease friends that the **trades** were a better bet than university.
think: I think supermarket **freezers keep breaking** whatever happens with AI.
I think having **two trades** at home makes us secure.
do: Keep at my **licence** and lead more call-outs with Hendrik.
Keep saving for a **house** with Pieter.
Take a course on **commercial kitchen equipment**.
S0.quote: Supermarket freezers break down at 2 a.m. whether or not anyone believes in AI, and someone has to drive out and fix them.
fieldNote: Dana's **varied repair work** and a plumber partner give her real security.
She uses AI lightly, for **fault codes**, and checks with Hendrik.
Her plans are **traditional**: marry, house near her parents, children.

steps.text: Lead more call-outs with Hendrik as backup
Keep adding to the house deposit pot with Pieter
Take a short course on commercial kitchen equipment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning, booking, answering customers. That's our helpdesk, the people who send us the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's tough for office workers, but there's always work for people who can fix things. I'd say this is why apprenticeships matter. I'd encourage my cousin's kids to look at trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the bit that changes is the stuff around the job. When the supermarket's own sensors spot a failing fridge before it breaks, there are fewer 2 a.m. call-outs, and less overtime for me. The repair work itself, though, I still do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI more for fault-finding, once Hendrik and the others are using it. I'd pick up weekend jobs with Pieter, bathrooms that need both a plumber and an electrician, to make up lost overtime. I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Overtime is about a fifth of what I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the helpdesk would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margit, who sends me most of my jobs. She knows which stores are fussy and which managers to avoid. If a computer replaces her, it'll send me to the wrong door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the weekend jobs be a big change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, we already do a few for family. We'd just do them for strangers too, properly, with invoices.

say: I'd say there's always work for **people who fix things**.
I'd say this is why **apprenticeships** matter, and urge young cousins into trades.
think: I think **store sensors** will cut 2 a.m. call-outs and overtime.
I think the **repair work** itself still stays with me.
do: Use **AI for fault-finding** once others do.
Take **weekend bathroom jobs** with Pieter, with invoices.
feel: I feel **a bit uneasy**; overtime is a fifth of my pay.
S1.quote: When the supermarket's own sensors spot a failing fridge before it breaks, there are fewer 2 a.m. call-outs, and less overtime for me.
fieldNote: Dana sees sensors cutting **overtime**, not her core job.
She worries for **Margit** on the helpdesk, who knows every store.
Weekend work with Pieter is a **natural extension**, not a leap.

steps.text: Use AI to read fault codes once Hendrik's team does
Take paid weekend bathroom jobs with Pieter, with proper invoices
Keep saving for the house at the same rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for thinking AI, and robots by 2031. That's quicker than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together, and people shouldn't wait for government. I'd say hard work and good skills will still count. I'd keep my doubts to myself, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine until 2031, maybe even busier. A robot that can carry boxes round a warehouse is a long way from a robot that can find why a pizza oven trips at noon. But if they get there by 2031, Pieter and I are both in trouble at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence in the first year and then the refrigeration qualification, because that's complex. Pieter and I would hold off on the house and save harder, maybe 500 a month together. We'd keep doing weekend jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not terrified, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Both of you in trades at once. What's the plan if both jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move closer to my parents, maybe into their spare room for a while, and save the rent. My dad would like the company. It's not ideal, but family is there for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put off the wedding too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the wedding's happening. It'd just be smaller, in the village hall. That's not something I'd let a robot decide.

say: I'd say families and communities must **pull together**.
I'd say hard work and **good skills** still count, and keep doubts private.
think: I think I'm fine until **2031**, maybe busier.
I fear **Pieter and I** both get hit at once.
do: Get my **licence**, then a refrigeration qualification.
Hold off the **house** and save 500 a month together.
S2.quote: A robot that can carry boxes round a warehouse is a long way from a robot that can find why a pizza oven trips at noon.
fieldNote: Dana notices that **two trades** at home could be hit together.
She'd fall back on **family**, not government.
The **wedding** stays on, just smaller, in the village hall.

steps.text: Take the refrigeration qualification after the licence
Pause the house purchase and save 500 a month with Pieter
Hold a smaller wedding in the village hall
Keep weekend jobs going with Pieter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots in 2034. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when you get trained up properly, do your apprenticeship, earn your licence. I'd say the people who prepare will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to become properly skilled, not junior. By 2034 I want to be the electrician the supermarket calls when the robot can't work out what's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the licence and the refrigeration qualification, then start my own small firm with Pieter in a few years, doing bathrooms and kitchens. We'd buy the house in the village in three years. I'd use AI when it's clearly helpful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious about the robots in 2034, but mostly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own firm? That's new.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's been in the back of my mind. Pieter and I work well together. If the big contractors bring in robots, small local firms doing awkward jobs might do better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would scare you off doing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt. I wouldn't borrow for it. We'd start with the van we have and the tools we own.

say: I'd say this is when you **get trained properly** and earn your licence.
I'd say people who **prepare** will be fine.
think: I think I'd have time to become **properly skilled**.
I want to be the electrician called when **the robot can't** fix it.
do: Start a **small firm with Pieter** in a few years.
Buy the **village house** in three years.
feel: I feel **mostly ready**, with some worry about 2034.
S3.quote: By 2034 I want to be the electrician the supermarket calls when the robot can't work out what's wrong.
fieldNote: Dana's plan grows to a **firm with Pieter**, with no borrowing.
She bets on **awkward local jobs** outlasting robots.
Five years lets her keep the **house plan**.

steps.text: Start a small bathroom and kitchen firm with Pieter, without borrowing
Get the licence and refrigeration qualification

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. I'd be nearly 40, married, kids hopefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so plan, train, and look after your family. That's what my dad would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be settled by then. Ten years is enough to get the house, the wedding and two kids, and only then do I have to worry about robots. It's the kids I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the licence, then the refrigeration qualification, and stay with the maintenance contractor a few years. We'd marry in two years and buy the house. Maybe start the firm later, maybe not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about what our kids would do, not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, but learn the computers too. My dad only knew engines, and I want them to know both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd change sooner, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving into a pension now, not in my thirties. It's boring, but it's the one thing I'd regret.

say: I'd say **plan, train**, and look after your family.
I'd repeat what **my dad** would say about a decade being long.
think: I think I'd be **settled** by then, with house and wedding done.
I'd worry more about **our kids** than about us.
do: Marry in two years and buy **the house**.
Start a **pension** now, not in my thirties.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about our future kids' work.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to get the house, the wedding and two kids, and only then do I have to worry about robots.
fieldNote: Dana's worry shifts to the **next generation** with a long warning.
She wants her kids to learn **trades and computers**.
She'd start a **pension** early as the one regret to avoid.

steps.text: Start paying into a pension this year
Marry Pieter in two years and buy the village house
Stay with the maintenance contractor while finishing qualifications

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Pieter and I could both get hit at once around 2031. What would help is fast, proper apprenticeships for qualifications like refrigeration, and being near family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the night calls. People think electricians wire new houses, but half my job is a supermarket manager at 2 a.m. who needs his freezers back on.

headlineQuote: People think electricians wire new houses, but half my job is a supermarket manager at 2 a.m. who needs his freezers back on.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old junior** on a maintenance contractor's call-out team for supermarkets and restaurants.
Her partner Pieter is a **plumber**; they save for a village house near her parents.
She's steady with tech, using **AI for fault codes**, and believes in trades and family.
She grows anxious when **both trades** could be hit together, and plans a small firm with Pieter.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as both she and Pieter could be hit around 2031.
